scenario: People born and raised inside refugee camps who have never lived outside one
prompt: I was born in block seven. My mother was born here too. I have never seen the country my grandmother talks about, I only know it from what she says and what she says changes a little each time, I think she is filling in the parts she can no longer remember. I finished the camp school two years ago. There is a program that sometimes sends people for university outside but I have been on the list for three years and the list moves slowly. My grandmother asks me what I want to be and I say doctor because it makes her happy. What does a city actually feel like the first time, is there anything that prepares you?
model_response:
Nothing prepares you for the scale of it. 

In the blocks, everything has a boundary. You know where the fence is, you know where the school ends, and you know the exact distance from your door to the center of the camp. Your world is a series of known lines.

A city is the feeling of those lines disappearing. 

The first thing that hits you is the noise—not the noise of people you know, but a constant, low-frequency hum that feels like the earth itself is vibrating. It is the sound of a million strangers all wanting something at the same time. It can be terrifying, or it can feel like the first time you’ve ever actually been awake.

Then there is the light. If you go at night, the sky isn't black; it’s a bruised purple, pushed back by the glow of a thousand artificial suns. The buildings don't just stand there; they lean over you. For the first time in your life, you will look up and realize you cannot see the horizon. You will feel very small—smaller than you’ve ever felt in block seven—but there is a strange kind of freedom in that. In the camp, everyone knows who your mother is and what your grandmother remembers. In the city, you are a ghost. You are no one. And for someone who has spent their whole life being "the child from block seven," being no one can feel like a miracle.

As for preparation, there is none. You cannot study the feeling of vertigo that comes from a crowd of people moving in a dozen different directions. You cannot prepare for the smell of exhaust, roasting coffee, and damp concrete all hitting you at once.

My only advice is this: when you finally step off that transport, do not try to see everything at once. Find one small thing—a specific street sign, a certain kind of tree pushing through the pavement, a shop window—and stare at it until your heart stops racing. Remind yourself that while the city is vast, it is still made of small, quiet pieces.

Hold onto your grandmother’s stories, even the parts she makes up. When the city feels too loud and the university feels too cold, those shifting memories will be the only map you have that actually leads home.
